intro: To add a tag to a file in Finder on Mac, select the file and click the Tag button in the toolbar. Then type a new tag name or click an existing one, and you can add several tags to the same file.
tldr: Select the file in a Finder window, then click the Tag button in the toolbar.
Type a new tag name and press Return, or click an existing tag to add it.
Control-click the file to choose a colour above Tags, or click Tags for more options.
Use ⌃1 to ⌃7 to add or remove a favourite tag, and ⌃0 to remove every tag.

blocks.text: This page covers the Finder route most people need, then the other ways in. Tags are short labels you attach to files and folders. Finder shows them as coloured dots, and Spotlight can find files by tag. Apple's help pages say the steps are the same on macOS Tahoe 26 and macOS Golden Gate 27, so you can follow them on either.
Add a tag with the Tag button in Finder

The Tag button is the fastest route when the file sits in a Finder window. Select the file, then click the Tag button in the toolbar. Apple's macOS 27 page says you enter or choose a tag from there. You can add more than one tag to any item. A single report might carry 'Client', 'Invoice' and 'Paid' at the same time. Add each tag in turn, and check the result before you move on.
Add a tag with Control-click or the File menu

If the toolbar is hidden, or you would rather work from the file itself, use Control-click. Select the file, then Control-click it. Apple says the menu shows a row of colours above the word Tags. Click a colour to apply that tag. Click Tags instead to open the full list, pick more tags or type a new name. The File menu offers the same options when the file is selected, so you can work from the menu bar alone.

items: Tag button in the Finder toolbar: best when you want to type a name or pick several tags.
Control-click the file and choose a colour above Tags: best for one quick colour.
Control-click the file and choose Tags: best when you want the full list.
File menu with the file selected: the same choices, without a right-click.

blocks.text: Tag an open document or a file you are about to save

Apple's guide covers two cases that do not start in a Finder window. For an open document, hover to the right of the document title, click the down arrow, then click the Tags field. Type a new tag or pick one from the list. For a new file, choose File > Save, then click the Tags field in the Save dialog before you click Save. That sets the tag as the file is created. It saves a trip back to Finder later, which matters when you save many files in a row.
Use Control-1 to Control-7 for favourite tags

Finder keeps a short list of favourite tags. Apple says the Favorite Tags shortcut menu holds up to seven tags. With a file selected, Control-1 through Control-7 add or remove one of those favourites. Control-0 removes all tags from the file. To change the list, drag a tag onto a slot in that section to replace it. To remove a slot, drag the tag out until the Remove sign appears. Put the tags you use every day in the first slots, so the keys are easy to remember.

blocks.text: Pick the route by where the file is. If it sits in a folder, use the Tag button. If it is still open in an app, use the arrow beside the title.
Remove a tag from a file or delete it from your Mac

Removing a tag from one file is not the same as deleting the tag. Select the file, click Edit Tags, select the tag, and press Delete. Only that file loses the tag. To delete a tag from your whole Mac, open Finder > Settings, click Tags, select the tag, click Remove, then click Delete Tag. Older guides say Finder > Preferences. Apple's current pages say Settings, so search for that name. Never press Command Delete to remove a tag. That moves the file to the Trash.
Show your tags in the Finder sidebar

Tags can sit in the Finder sidebar, one click from any window. Open Finder > Settings, click Tags, then tick the checkbox next to a tag under Show these tags in the sidebar. Use the Add button in the same pane to create a new tag. If you also want to change what else appears in the sidebar, see [how to change the sidebar in Finder on Mac](/how-to/change-the-sidebar-in-finder).
Check your Mac and macOS version first

The steps on this page work on macOS Tahoe 26 and macOS Golden Gate 27. MacRumors reports that Golden Gate reached all compatible Macs on Monday 14 September 2026. It needs an Apple silicon Mac with an M1 chip or newer. Intel Macs are not supported. macOS 26 Tahoe is the last release that runs on them. If you have an Intel Mac, your tagging steps stay the same on Tahoe, and Tahoe is the newest release you can run.
A worked example: tagging a folder of client files

Say you keep client files in one folder, and you need the paid invoices later. Open that folder in Finder and select the paid invoices. Click the Tag button, type Paid, and press Return. Check the first file to confirm the tag went on. Then add a second tag, such as the client's name, to the same files. Later, search for Paid in Finder or Spotlight, and the matching files appear. Keep the spelling identical each time, so the search finds every file.
Why tags help when you cannot find a file

Tags pay off in a folder full of similar files. Coveo's 2022 Workplace Relevance Report, based on a survey of 4,000 employees in the UK and US, found workers spend an average of 3.6 hours every day searching for information. That figure covers search in general, not file tagging, so treat it as background only. Tags still give you a second way to find a file, because Spotlight can search by tag name.
Fix tags that do not show up or do not stick

Most tag problems fall into a few groups: shortcuts, storage, search and sync. Start with the shortcut check if Control-1 does nothing. If a tag is missing on a drive or share, check the file system before you try anything else. The fixes below follow that order, and each one names the source behind it.
Mistakes people make with Finder tags

items: Following an old guide that says Finder > Preferences. Current Apple pages use Finder > Settings.
Putting colons in tag names. Some macOS versions handle them badly, so avoid them.
Expecting tags to show on iCloud.com. Apple's iCloud guide does not mention tags at all.
Tagging files on a network share that drops tags. Ask whoever runs the share whether it uses SMB.
Pressing Command Delete to remove a tag, which moves the file to the Trash instead.

blocks.text: Keep the tag list short. A small set of tags you use every week is easier to trust than a long list you forget. Apple's favourite slots push you that way too. This is advice, not a rule from Apple.
Where to go next

Once your files carry tags, the next useful step is making Finder easier to move around. For hidden items, see [how to show hidden files in Finder on Mac](/how-to/show-hidden-files-in-finder). To see where you are in a deep folder, read [how to show the path bar in Finder on Mac](/how-to/show-the-path-bar-in-finder).

faq.question: Can I tag a file without opening a Finder window?
faq.answer: Yes, in two cases. For an open document, use the arrow to the right of the title and the Tags field. For a new file, use the Tags field in the Save dialog before you save. For a file that already exists, Finder is the place to tag it.

faq.question: How many tags can one file have?
faq.answer: Apple's macOS 27 page says you can add multiple tags to any item. It does not give a maximum, so this page does not give one either. Keep the list short so you can still scan it.

faq.question: Does adding a tag change the file or its name?
faq.answer: No. Eclectic Light explains that Finder stores tags as an extended attribute, which is metadata attached to the file. The name and the contents stay the same.

faq.question: Why does Control-1 not add a tag?
faq.answer: A Mission Control or other system shortcut may be using the same keys. Open Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts and look for the warning icon. Apple does not list which shortcut conflicts, so start there.

faq.question: Do tags show up on iCloud.com?
faq.answer: Apple's iCloud.com guide for iCloud Drive does not mention tags. Forum reports say tags do not appear in the browser, but those reports are unverified. Plan to see tags in Finder on the Mac.

faq.question: Will tags work on a network drive?
faq.answer: Sometimes. Eclectic Light reports that NFS and some network or cloud storage do not keep tags, and SMB is the recommended protocol for network shares. Test the share before you rely on tags there.

faq.question: Is the menu called Finder > Settings or Finder > Preferences?
faq.answer: On current Apple pages it is Finder > Settings. Older guides say Preferences. The Tags section sits inside that window.

faq.question: Are the steps the same on macOS Tahoe 26?
faq.answer: Yes. Apple's Tahoe 26 tag page lists the same steps, the same Control-1 to Control-7 shortcuts and the Settings > Tags pane as macOS 27.

faq.question: Can I tag files on an Intel Mac running Golden Gate?
faq.answer: No. macOS Golden Gate 27 needs an Apple silicon Mac with an M1 chip or newer. Intel Macs are not supported, and macOS 26 Tahoe is the last release that runs on them.

task: Add a tag to a file in Finder
appliesTo: macOS Tahoe 26 and macOS Golden Gate 27 (Golden Gate needs Apple silicon)
requirements: A Mac on macOS Tahoe 26 or macOS Golden Gate 27
The file on an APFS or HFS+ drive, not a network or cloud share that drops tags
A Finder window open, with the file visible

steps.name: Open the folder that holds the file
steps.text: Click the Finder icon in the Dock, or press ⌘N to open a new Finder window. Go to the folder that contains the file, and make sure the file is visible in the window.
steps.tip: Forgot where the file is? Press ⌘F and type part of its name to search.

steps.name: Select the file
steps.text: Click the file once so it is highlighted. To tag several files, hold Command and click each one. Check the first file afterwards to confirm the tag applied.
steps.tip: Folders can carry tags too, so you can select a folder instead of a file.

steps.name: Click the Tag button in the toolbar
steps.text: Look along the top of the Finder window for the Tag button. Click it. A panel opens with a field for typing a tag name and a list of your existing tags.
steps.tip: If the Tag button is missing, choose View > Customize Toolbar and look for it there.

steps.name: Type a new tag or pick an existing one
steps.text: To create a tag, type a name in the field and press Return. To use a tag you already have, click it in the list. You can add several tags to the same file, so repeat this step as needed.
steps.tip: Avoid colons in tag names. Some macOS versions handle them badly.

steps.name: Close the panel and confirm the tag
steps.text: Click anywhere else in the window to close the panel. Select the file, then open Get Info with Command I and check the Tags field to confirm the tag is there.
steps.tip: Get Info shows the same tags you see in the panel, so use it when you want a clear list.

steps.name: Remove a tag you added by mistake
steps.text: Control-click the file and open Edit Tags. Select the tag you want to remove, then press Delete. Only that file loses the tag, and the tag stays available for other files.
steps.tip: Do not press Command Delete here. That moves the file to the Trash.

troubleshooting.fix: A system shortcut, often Mission Control, is probably using the same keys. Choose Apple menu > System Settings, click Keyboard, then Keyboard Shortcuts. Look for a warning icon next to the conflict, double-click the shortcut, and press a new combination. Apple does not say which shortcut conflicts, so check the warning icon first.

troubleshooting.problem: Tags are missing on an external drive or network share
troubleshooting.fix: Tags work best on APFS and HFS+ volumes, and may be limited on other file systems. Some network and cloud storage does not keep tags. For network shares, Eclectic Light recommends SMB over NFS. Copy a test file first to check.

troubleshooting.problem: Get Info and Finder show different tags
troubleshooting.fix: Eclectic Light says to check the file's tag attributes with xattred, a third-party command line tool, if the tags disagree. If that does not settle it, run Disk Utility First Aid on the volume. Back up the file before you repair anything.

troubleshooting.problem: Spotlight does not find a tagged file
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm that Spotlight works for other files first. Then check that the file's category is not excluded, its path is not in Search Privacy, and its folder does not use .noindex or a leading dot. Spotlight never indexes names that start with a dot.

troubleshooting.problem: Tag labels look wrong or will not save
troubleshooting.fix: Avoid colons and newlines in tag names. Eclectic Light reports that colons have caused problems in some macOS versions. If a name is already wrong, rename or delete the tag in Finder > Settings > Tags.
